# Is the floating_base_weight larger always better?

> **Current answer:** Not. When the contact force peak increases from 1e-6 to 1e6, it rises from 80 N to 110 N and the base speed fluctuations decrease. However, after reaching 1e14, large unstable contact force peaks and falling occur. A scan of contact force, velocity, and constraint residuals should be performed within a limited range, rather than increasing monotonically.

## Key terms

- Whole-Body Control (WBC) (全身控制)
- Quadratic Programming (QP) (二次规划)
- Model Predictive Control (MPC) (模型预测控制)
- Joint Torque (关节力矩)
- Latency Jitter (时延抖动)
- Dynamics (动力学)

## Problem and symptoms

- The MPC contact force penalty weight is too large, leading to insufficient support force; the WBC floating base weight is too large, leading to unstable contact force.
- Contact force is too small when mpc_alpha=0.1.
- Contact force becomes sparse and large when floating_base_weight=1e14, leading to falling.

## Environment

- Four-legged robot trot simulation; robot mass example is ~20 kg, total gravity ~200 N.

## Priority diagnostics

- Compare contact force, base angular velocity, and linear velocity curves under different weights.

## Possible causes

- mpc_alpha is a force amplitude penalty term; too large suppresses contact force; too small may amplify the sensitivity of the real robot to acceleration changes.
- The overlarge floating_base_weight excessively lowers the relaxation cost between dynamics and contact force.

## Attempts

- Test mpc_alpha=0.1, 0.0002 and ~5e-5; test floating_base_weight=1e-6, 1e6, 1e14.

## Effective fixes

- Reduce mpc_alpha to a level that can generate near-single-foot half-body contact force during the trot phase, and limitively increase floating_base_weight.

## Result

- Contact force peak of the foot increases from 80 N to 110 N when floating_base_weight increases from 1e-6 to 1e6, and base speed fluctuations decrease. However, when floating_base_weight is increased to 1e14, instability and falling occur.

## Limitations

- Numerical results from a specific four-legged simulation, and the author explicitly states that the conclusion is still to be verified by others; cannot directly be copied to human-like robots or different normalized cost functions.

## Safety notes

- The weight scan must set limits on contact force, torque, and state; the 1e14 scale has already caused falling in simulation, and cannot be directly implemented on real machines.

## Image and visual evidence

- Image 'mpc_alpha=0.1' simultaneously shows four-legged simulation and foot contact force curve; the curve amplitude is low, consistent with the text's description of insufficient support force, but the screenshot itself does not provide a uniform coordinate scale.
- Image 'floating_base_weight=1e6' shows a regular, periodic foot contact force waveform with peak around 110 N; this can be compared with the text's description of ~80 N at 1e-6.
- Image 'floating_base_weight=1e14' shows sparse and large contact force peaks, corresponding to the text's description of unstable contact force and falling.

## Applicability boundary

- This case is a single four-legged simulation observation, and the parameter scan must be re-done within the cost scaling of the target controller.
